title: Houthi Missiles Pierce Saudi Air Defenses as Riyadh Activates Its Turkey-Pakistan Defense Pact
subhead: Repeat Houthi cruise and ballistic missile strikes on Riyadh's King Khalid airport killed 14 across two days and exposed the interceptor-supply math behind Gulf air defense, while the $77B US submarine award and a $100M drone order showed procurement continuing at pace.

sections.heading: Riyadh Airport Hit Twice in Two Days as Houthi Missiles Beat Saudi Air Defense
sections.body:
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis struck Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on consecutive days, according to Reuters and The Guardian. Saturday's missile attack killed 13 people and injured more than 300 — described by The Guardian as the deadliest attack on a Gulf state since the US-Iran war began in March. On Sunday an unidentified projectile hit Terminal 4, killing one person and injuring 11; Saudi air defenses intercepted a cruise missile near the airport, per Syrian state outlet SANA. Saudi authorities confirmed a separate attack on King Fahd airport in Dammam.

The Houthis claimed to have used two cruise missiles on the airport, and warned airlines and travellers to avoid Saudi airports and airspace, saying 'the worst is yet to come.' The Saudi-led coalition spokesperson, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the coalition would 'respond firmly.' Saudi authorities extended the Riyadh airport closure and moved schools online until Thursday.
sections.whyItMatters: The strikes show a non-state actor repeatedly landing cruise and ballistic missiles on a capital's primary airport despite one of the most heavily funded air-defense networks in the region — a live test of the interceptor-supply economics now shaping Gulf procurement.

sections.heading: The Interceptor Math: Why Saudi Defense Spending Has Not Bought Immunity
sections.body:
Al Jazeera's explainer and a National Herald India analysis both zero in on the same dynamic: the Houthis need only occasional breakthroughs, while Saudi Arabia must simultaneously defend airports, cities, military sites, oil facilities and sea lanes. Even successful intercepts consume scarce Patriot and other interceptor stocks — and the analysis cites reports of dwindling US interceptor supplies. That asymmetry, not a lack of hardware, is the core problem.

This lands directly on procurement policy. The past week alone saw Lockheed Martin unveil its PAC-3 Edge interceptor pitched at hypersonic and advanced threats, Boeing win a contract worth up to $14.7 billion to build PAC-3 MSE seekers, and RTX's Raytheon win up to $6.3 billion to produce Standard Missile-3 Block IB interceptors — all Reuters-reported moves to rebuild missile-defense inventories. The Riyadh strikes are the demand signal those awards answer.
sections.whyItMatters: Interceptor inventories, not launcher counts, are the binding constraint in sustained air defense. The US industrial base is being asked to fund that gap — and the Gulf is the first customer watching whether it can actually deliver.

sections.heading: Makkah Pact Activated: Turkey and Pakistan Drawn Toward the Gulf
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia formally activated the Makkah defense pact on 5 October, committing Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan to collective defense obligations, according to a National Herald India analysis. Reuters reported Turkey is sending mainly defensive and technical support to help fight the Houthis after the three countries pledged to act on the pact's collective-defense clause.

The analysis stresses the operational limits: activation does not mean Turkish or Pakistani troops are in combat, Pakistan's defense minister described its role as supportive, and Turkey's parliament has yet to ratify the agreement. Intelligence sharing, training and air defense are the plausible contributions — capabilities that protect Saudi territory without deploying allied troops into Yemen, but which also free Saudi forces for offensive operations.
sections.whyItMatters: A nuclear-armed Pakistan and NATO-member Turkey signing onto Gulf collective defense widens the coalition structure around the Yemen conflict without yet committing boots — a political signal to Iran and the Houthis whose operational weight remains unproven.

sections.heading: US Navy Locks In $77B for 14 Nuclear Submarines
sections.body: The US Navy awarded nearly $77 billion in contract modifications to General Dynamics Electric Boat and HII Newport News Shipbuilding for nine Virginia-class attack submarines and five Columbia-class ballistic-missile submarines, per Eurasia Review. The Columbia package totals $29.5 billion; the Virginia Block VI package $42.1 billion, carrying the 84-foot Virginia Payload Module for Tomahawk and future hypersonic weapons. The Navy will reclassify VPM-equipped boats from SSN to SSGN. Seven Columbias are already under contract, with the first due in 2028.
sections.whyItMatters: This is industrial-base policy as much as procurement: the awards lock in continuous submarine production capacity for years and tie the most survivable leg of the US nuclear triad to a two-yard supply chain that has struggled with throughput.

sections.heading: Pentagon's $1B Drone Dominance Program Names Its Biggest Winner
sections.body:
Neros Technologies won the largest single order of the Pentagon's Gauntlet II round — 14,000 Archer attack drones valued at more than $100 million, per SOFREP. The order splits into 8,000 five-inch Archer FPVs for close-quarters battle and 6,000 ten-inch Archer AI with terminal guidance and GPS-denied position hold. Neros also received 800 drones reallocated from competitors that missed earlier delivery deadlines. Delivery pace, not test scores alone, now gates awards.

The program sits inside the Pentagon's Drone Dominance effort — described by Ken Klippenstein's newsletter as a $1 billion plan for 340,000 small attack drones over two years, with unit prices meant to fall from $5,000 toward $2,300. On the counter-drone side, Ukraine's Phantom Defense demonstrated its Specter EW suite and Streamhunter video-interception system at Gauntlet II, claiming all radio-controlled platforms tested were disrupted, per the Kyiv Post.
sections.whyItMatters: The Pentagon is buying attritable drones by the tens of thousands and counter-drone EW from a combat-tested Ukrainian supplier — a shift from exquisite platforms toward mass, expendable systems and the electronic warfare that beats them.

sections.heading: Ukraine's Drone Industry Goes Venture-Scale — and Moves West
sections.body: Kyiv drone maker Airlogix is in talks to raise $100 million at a valuation above $2 billion, Forbes reported, which would make it the most valuable company to emerge from Ukraine's post-2022 defense industry. Founder Vitalii Kolesnichenko said Russian strikes destroyed its production sites more than once, pushing manufacturing into Germany, Canada and the UK, with joint ventures including a German tie-up with Auterion producing the Seth X and Anubis strike drones. Handelsblatt put the German contract at roughly 300 million euros ($349 million) for over 5,000 airframes.
sections.whyItMatters: Ukraine's wartime drone makers are becoming investable, geographically distributed suppliers to European militaries — turning battlefield necessity into a durable Western defense-industrial capability outside Ukraine's borders.

sections.heading: India's Fifth-Gen Fighter Choice Stays Open — Russia Offers Su-57, US Has Not Formally Offered F-35
sections.body: IAF Chief Air Chief Marshal AP Singh said the US has made no formal offer to sell India the F-35, and that no decision has been taken on Russia's proposal to supply the Su-57, per Business Standard. He spoke in Jodhpur alongside US Pacific Air Forces commander Gen Kevin Schneider at the close of exercise Tarang Shakti-2026, where the F-35 flew for the first time. Singh noted Indian personnel were shown the jet but not its cockpit. Both officers confirmed Operation Sindoor was discussed with participating nations, including the US, France, Germany and Australia.
sections.whyItMatters: India is keeping two rival fifth-generation options alive while pursuing an indigenous program — a deliberate hedge that leaves both Washington and Moscow bidding for one of the world's largest fighter markets.

bottomLine: The day's defining story is the mismatch between spending and protection: Saudi Arabia, one of the world's most heavily armed air-defense customers, could not stop repeat Houthi missile strikes on its capital's airport, and the fix — more interceptors, faster — is exactly what the past week's PAC-3, MSE and SM-3 awards are meant to deliver. Riyadh answered politically by activating its Turkey-Pakistan collective-defense pact, a widening of the Yemen conflict's coalition structure whose operational weight is still unproven. Elsewhere, procurement marched on: a $77 billion US submarine package locks in undersea production for years, the Pentagon handed its biggest Drone Dominance order to Neros, Ukraine's Airlogix chased a $2 billion valuation while relocating production westward, and India kept both the F-35 and Su-57 in play. The throughline is inventory and industrial capacity — who can produce and sustain enough interceptors, submarines and drones to matter in prolonged conflict.
sources: Reuters, The Guardian, Al Jazeera, SANA (Syria), National Herald India, Eurasia Review, SOFREP, Kyiv Post/Militarnyi, DroneXL/Forbes, Business Standard, Ken Klippenstein, Economic Times
